definition: The basic unit of text a language model processes — roughly a word piece, not always a whole word.
example: The word 'unbelievable' might be split into a few tokens rather than counted as one, depending on the model's tokenizer.
commonMisconception: A token is always one character or one word. In practice it varies by language, model, and word.
relevance: Context windows and API usage are both measured in tokens, not words or characters.

definition: Standing instructions given to a model before the conversation starts, shaping its behaviour for every turn that follows.
example: Claude Code's own default behaviours (like asking before risky actions) come from instructions set outside the visible chat, similar in spirit to a system prompt.
commonMisconception: A system prompt guarantees the model will never deviate from it. It strongly influences behaviour but is not an unbreakable rule enforced outside the model itself.
relevance: Distinguishes 'instructions the model was given' from 'permissions the tool actually enforces' — a distinction this course keeps returning to.
